tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

# New host runbook

From a blank machine to an Arch box running this flake. Everything after
booting the stick happens over SSH, so it can be driven from another machine.

The result: full-disk LUKS2 → btrfs (`@`, `@home`, `@nix`, `@log`, `@cache`,
zstd), systemd-boot, NetworkManager, user `sauyon` in `wheel`, Determinate Nix,
and the first Home Manager switch done.

## 0. Register the host in the flake

Pick a hostname, then in this repo:

- `flake.nix`: add `homeConfigurations.<host> = linuxHome { hostname = "<host>"; gui = true; };`
  (`gpu = "amd"`/`"nvidia"` only if it has one; anything else can be left out).
- `home.nix`: add `<host>` to the `hms` CI case (`utsuho|setsuna|...`) if it
  gets a CI job, and to whichever scale knob its panel wants: `hidpi` for 1.25
  app-level scaling, or `laptopScale` for a 2x compositor scale on `eDP-1`.
  Pick one — they multiply.
- `.forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml`: add
  `.#homeConfigurations.<host>.activationPackage` to the build step.
- `system/deploy`: add `<host>` to the host case in the *host packages* step.
  It is an allow-list on purpose — a box we don't own the OS of must not get
  handed packages — so a host missing from it silently skips that step and says
  so when you run the deploy.

Commit and push; CI will have the closure in attic by the time you need it.

## 1. Build the install ISO

`install/` holds an archiso profile overlay on top of the stock `releng`
profile. The ISO auto-joins one Wi-Fi network (iwd) and allows key-only root
SSH, advertised over mDNS as `archiso.local`. Needs Docker (Docker Desktop is
fine; the build runs in a privileged `archlinux` container).

```bash
cp install/wifi.env.example install/wifi.env   # set WIFI_SSID / WIFI_PASSPHRASE
mise run host:iso                               # --out <dir>, default ~/Downloads
```

It uses `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` as the root key unless `install/authorized_keys`
already exists. Both files are gitignored. The Wi-Fi passphrase ends up in
plain text inside the ISO — treat the ISO file accordingly.

## 2. Write it to a stick and boot

`dd` it (or Rufus in DD mode on Windows) and **verify by reading it back** — a
flaky stick or port produced scattered bad blocks once and the result would
not have booted reliably. Compare `sha256sum` of the ISO against the same
number of bytes read from the device.

On the new host: **disable Secure Boot** (archiso isn't signed; the failure
shows up as a bare "EFI boot failed"), then boot the `UEFI:` entry.

Find it with `ssh root@archiso.local`. If mDNS doesn't resolve, scan for SSH
(`nmap -p22 --open <lan>/24`) and pick the `OpenSSH` banner, or read `ip a`
off its screen.

## 3. Base install

Check the target disk first (`lsblk`) — the script refuses a disk that
already has partitions, so wipe it by hand (`sgdisk -Z`) only when you mean it.

```bash
mise run host:install <ip> <host>     # --disk <dev>, default /dev/nvme0n1
```

**On an AMD box pass `--hw`**, or it gets Intel microcode and Intel video
drivers:

```bash
mise run host:install <ip> <host> --hw 'amd-ucode vulkan-radeon libva-mesa-driver'
```

The package set is two files plus that flag: `system/packages` (what every host
must have — `system/deploy` keeps enforcing it afterwards),
`install/packages-install-only` (base, kernel, and enough shell to reach
`bootstrap`; never re-enforced), and `--hw` for the parts that would be wrong on
the other architecture. Both lists are scp'd to the ISO alongside the script.

--- system/packages ---
# Host (pacman) packages that must be PRESENT for this config to work.
# system/deploy converges pacman onto this file on every run, on the hosts its
# own allow-list names, so a line added here reaches setsuna/utsuho/shiori on
# their next `mise run system:deploy` -- which is the point. pacstrap's list only
# ever reached the *next* new box, which is how fprintd stayed uninstalled for
# months after being wired up in hyprlock and pam.d.
#
# What belongs here: things that must be root-side, because a user profile
# cannot provide them -- a system systemd unit, a system D-Bus service, a module
# the host's own libraries dlopen by name, firmware, state under /var. Anything
# a user can own belongs in home.nix.
#
# What does NOT belong here, and lives in install/packages-install-only instead:
# anything only a *fresh install* needs. The kernel especially -- enforcing
# `linux` would install a second, stock kernel on a host running linux-lts or
# -zen -- and the shell tools install-base.sh needs before home-manager exists.
# That file is pacstrapped once and never enforced again.
#
# Hardware packages sort by whether being wrong is harmful or merely inert:
# intel-ucode and the Intel video drivers are picked per host and stay inline in
# install-base.sh, because pushing them at the AMD boxes would be wrong; fprintd
# and sof-firmware sit here, because a box without the hardware just never
# exercises them.
#
# Format: one package per line, # comments, blank lines ignored. Package names
# only -- `pacman -Qq` resolves virtual provides (`sh` answers bash) but NOT
# groups, so a group line would read as missing on every single deploy.

# disks: the encrypted btrfs root and the ESP
btrfs-progs
cryptsetup
dosfstools

# network and remote access
networkmanager
openssh
sudo

# The account's login shell is the absolute path /bin/zsh (install-base.sh's
# useradd -s), which no nix profile can provide -- home.nix owns zsh's
# configuration, not that path. So the binary is a host package.
zsh

# graphics
mesa

# audio
sof-firmware
pipewire
pipewire-pulse
pipewire-alsa
wireplumber

# firmware blobs for the kernel, whichever kernel that is
linux-firmware

# system services
polkit
tpm2-tss
tpm2-tools
bluez
bluez-utils
fwupd
power-profiles-daemon

# Fingerprint reader (Goodix 27c6:609c on shiori). Cannot come from nix: the
# host's PAM dlopens pam_fprintd.so by bare name out of /usr/lib/security (see
# etc/pam.d/polkit-1), fprintd itself is a root-run system D-Bus service, and
# its enrollments are root state in /var/lib/fprint. hyprlock's
# fingerprint.enabled (home.nix) reaches the daemon over D-Bus rather than PAM,
# so it silently no-ops when the package is absent.
# Enrolling stays manual and per-host: `fprintd-enroll`, then `fprintd-list`.
fprintd

packages

**What I found first (grounds the questions):**

2. Nothing work-specific is gated on `setsuna` today — `pkgs.slack` (`home.nix:2285`), the Modular sops keys (`home.nix:1443`), coder→`rde.modular.com`, and the `work` Claude profile are on **every** host. The only setsuna-only bits are DPI (`hidpi`/`dconf`, `home.nix:2695`) and a kanshi profile.

One honest flag up front, then I'll stop: **distrobox is not a security boundary.** It creates containers with `--privileged`, host network, host IPC and host PID. If you ever want the sandbox reading of "isolate", that's a VM, not this.

result_command="${container_manager} create"
	result_command="${result_command} ${container_platform}"
	# use the host's namespace for ipc, network, pid, ulimit
	result_command="${result_command}
		--hostname \"${container_hostname}\"
		--name \"${container_name}\"
		--privileged
		--security-opt label=disable
		--security-opt apparmor=unconfined
		--pids-limit=-1
		--user root:root"

	if [ "${unshare_ipc}" -eq 0 ]; then
		result_command="${result_command}
			--ipc host"
	# We also mount host's root filesystem to /run/host, to be able to syphon
	# dynamic configurations from the host.
	#
	# Mount user home, dev and host's root inside container.
	# This grants access to external devices like usb webcams, disks and so on.
	#
	# Mount also the distrobox-init utility as the container entrypoint.
	# Also mount in the container the distrobox-export and distrobox-host-exec
	# utilities.
	result_command="${result_command}
		--label \"manager=distrobox\"
		--label \"distrobox.unshare_groups=${unshare_groups}\"
		--env \"SHELL=$(basename "${SHELL:-"/bin/bash"}")\"
		--env \"HOME=${container_user_home}\"
		--env \"container=${container_manager}\"
		--env \"TERMINFO_DIRS=/usr/share/terminfo:/run/host/usr/share/terminfo\"
		--env \"CONTAINER_ID=${container_name}\"
		--volume /tmp:/tmp${rslave}
		--volume \"${distrobox_entrypoint_path}\":/usr/bin/entrypoint:ro
		--volume \"${distrobox_export_path}\":/usr/bin/distrobox-export:ro
		--volume \"${distrobox_hostexec_path}\":/usr/bin/distrobox-host-exec:ro
		--volume \"${container_user_home}\":\"${container_user_home}\"${rslave}"

	# Due to breaking change in https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/commit/d4b670fca6d0ac606777376440ffe49686ce15f4
	# now we cannot mount /:/run/host as before, as it will try to mount RO partitions as RW thus breaking things.
	# This will ensure we will mount directories one-by-one thus avoiding this problem.
	#
	# This happens ONLY with podman+runc, docker and lilipod are unaffected, so let's do this only if we have podman AND runc.
	if echo "${container_manager}" | grep -q "podman" && ${container_manager} info 2> /dev/null | grep -q runc > /dev/null 2>&1; then
		for rootdir in /*; do

			# Skip symlinks
			if [ -L "${rootdir}" ]; then
				continue
			fi

			# Find if the directory belongs to a RO mount, if do, mount it as RO+Rslave
			if findmnt --notruncate --noheadings --list --output OPTIONS --target "${rootdir}" |
				tr ',' '\n' | grep -q "^ro$"; then

				result_command="${result_command}
				--volume ${rootdir}:/run/host${rootdir}:ro${rslave}"
				continue
			fi

			# Else we mount it RW+Rslave
			result_command="${result_command}
				--volume ${rootdir}:/run/host${rootdir}${rslave}"
		done
	else
		# We're either on podman+crun, docker or lilipod, let's keep old behaviour
		result_command="${result_command}
			--volume /:/run/host/${rslave}"

	fi

	if [ "${unshare_devsys}" -eq 0 ]; then
		result_command="${result_command}
			--volume /dev:/dev${rslave}
			--volume /sys:/sys${rslave}"

content.text:
**Verdict first: `distrobox --home` does not do what you want.** Read the source, not the docs:

1. `distrobox-create:734` unconditionally adds `--volume "$HOME:$HOME"` using the **host** home — `--home` never removes it.
2. `distrobox-create:891-893` shows what `--home` actually does: overrides `$HOME`, adds a second mount, and helpfully exports `DISTROBOX_HOST_HOME` pointing back at `/home/sauyon`.
3. `distrobox-create:754-765` mounts host `/` at `/run/host` regardless. `--unshare-all` (lines 342-348) covers ipc/netns/process/devsys/groups — **not** the home mount.
4. Every container gets `--privileged --security-opt label=disable --security-opt apparmor=unconfined` (`:692-694`).

So a distrobox running as `sauyon` hands Falcon your home twice over.

**On your systemd-homed idea — right primitive, wrong mechanism.** Encryption protects data *at rest*; Falcon is a live process on an unlocked home, so it walks straight in. What actually protects you is the **separate UID**: run the box as a second user, and rootless podman maps container-root to *that* uid, so `/home/sauyon` (mode 0700) is unreadable even through `/run/host`. The encryption is a bonus, not the control. This repo already runs homed for `sauyon` (`system/storage-tuning.sh`), so `homectl create work --storage=luks` is idiomatic here.

**The problem with the plan:** Falcon can't work in a rootless container at all. Kprobe/tracepoint eBPF loads and module loading check capabilities in the *initial* user namespace, so a userns container refuses them no matter how privileged it looks. Contain Falcon and you break it; let it work and it sees everything. That fork is yours, not mine.

Two answers, one of which fights your own requirement — I'll flag it once and then do as you say.

**"Just use my user"** means the Falcon-can't-see-my-files goal is off the table *if* we use distrobox, for the reason I verified: `distrobox-create:734` mounts `$HOME` in, and there's no flag to stop it. Same-UID *can* still be made defensible, but only by dropping distrobox for hand-rolled podman (no `/run/host`, no `$HOME`, unshared PID ns, and only individual sockets mounted — never the session D-Bus, which is a trivial escape back into your userland). That's the trade: distrobox's easy-entry ergonomics exist *because* it fuses with the host.

## eBPF Backend and Kernel Module Requirements

The Falcon sensor for Linux uses extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) programs loaded from user space, eliminating the need for a kernel module. The sensor uses extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) programs that are loaded from the user space.

## User Mode Operation

User mode is the default mode when the Linux kernel doesn't meet the requirements for kernel mode but does support user mode. User mode can be enabled on hosts with kernels that meet specific requirements, including custom kernels.

## Architecture

The Linux sensor has two variants: one using eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter), and another using Linux kernel modules.

## Reduced Functionality Mode

If kernel requirements aren't met, RFM is a safe mode for the Falcon sensor that prevents compatibility issues if the host's kernel is unsupported by the sensor in kernel mode and doesn't meet the sensor's user mode requirements.

The search results indicate that while the sensor can operate in user mode with eBPF, the exact technical requirements for kernel version compatibility and specific eBPF features are not detailed in these sources. Here are the search results for "Falcon Container Sensor user mode requirements privileged capabilities rootless":

## Key Findings:

**User Mode Operation:**
The Falcon Container sensor runs as an unprivileged container in user space with no code running in the kernel of the worker node OS. This is a key distinction from the kernel-based Falcon sensor.

**Use Cases for User Mode:**
The Falcon Container sensor allows it to secure Kubernetes pods in clusters where it isn't possible to deploy the kernel-based Falcon sensor for Linux on the worker node, as with AWS Fargate where organizations don't have access to the kernel and where privileged containers are disallowed.

**Privileged vs. Unprivileged Deployment:**
In contrast, when deploying the Falcon Linux Sensor (container image) to Kubernetes nodes, it is a requirement that the Falcon Sensor run as a privileged container so that the Sensor can properly work with the kernel. This applies to the traditional kernel-based sensor, not the Container sensor.

**Rootless Compatibility:**
Flatcar Container Linux x86_64 (3139.2.2+, kernel 5.15.43-flatcar+) is supported in user/BPF mode. This indicates that user mode operation (which is compatible with rootless environments) is supported on specific platforms.

The Falcon Container Sensor is specifically designed for environments where privileged containers and kernel access are restricted, making it suitable for rootless and serverless container deployments.

content.text:
**Research verdict: "user mode" is a naming trap. It doesn't mean what you're hoping.**

1. CrowdStrike's "user mode" = the *sensor code* lives in user space and uses eBPF instead of a kernel module. It does **not** mean no kernel privileges. If neither mode's requirements are met the sensor drops to [Reduced Functionality Mode](https://oit.duke.edu/help/articles/kb0038677/).
2. CrowdStrike's own eBPF writeup says it plainly: "almost all eBPF-related actions require the `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or `CAP_BPF` capabilities, which in practical terms typically means running as root either on the host or inside a privileged container" ([CrowdStrike, Analyzing the Security of eBPF Maps](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/analyzing-the-security-of-ebpf-maps/)).
3. Rootless podman can't supply that. Capability checks for tracing program types (kprobe, tracepoint, perf_event) are made against the **initial** user namespace, so a userns container's `--privileged` caps don't count. Falcon would sit in RFM or fail to attach.
4. `falcon-helm`'s node deployment confirms the shape: `hostPID, hostIPC, hostNetwork, and a privileged container` ([falcon-helm README](https://github.com/CrowdStrike/falcon-helm/blob/main/helm-charts/falcon-sensor/README.md)).
5. The one genuinely kernel-free build is the [Falcon Container Sensor](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/everything-to-know-about-securing-containers-with-falcon/) — "runs as an unprivileged container in user space with no code running in the kernel of the worker node OS." But it's a Kubernetes/Fargate workload sensor injected as a sidecar, not an endpoint sensor for a laptop. It won't satisfy endpoint compliance.

**And going rootful collapses the whole idea:** podman as real root with `--privileged` makes Falcon work, and simultaneously hands it the host kernel, host PID namespace, and root-read of your entire disk. Strictly worse than either end of the fork.

**Your VM objection is wrong, though — in your favour.** `waypipe` proxies the Wayland protocol out of the guest, so guest apps appear as ordinary individual windows in Hyprland, not one big nested-desktop rectangle. A VM *can* spawn apps into your userland.

So there's no middle ground, and the fork is smaller than it looks: **if Falcon isn't in the box, you barely need containment** — the box would hold Slack/gcloud/mcloud, which you already run natively (`home.nix:2285`), so it's a tidiness boundary and distrobox-as-you is fine. **If Falcon is in the box, only a VM does it.**

Fair — and yes, measurably. Straight answer, then the thing that matters more.

**Battery: single-digit watts, but the framing matters.**

1. **Falcon is the cost, not the VM.** `falcon-sensor-bpf` continuously traces syscalls and is [well known for high CPU](https://inventivehq.com/knowledge-base/crowdstrike/falcon-sensor-bpf-high-cpu-usage). You pay that on setsuna today. Moving it to shiori moves the drain; it doesn't create it.
2. **The VM's own overhead is the new cost:** a second kernel's idle tick, virtio polling, and fewer deep package C-states for the host. On this box expect ~2–5W idle-with-Falcon — roughly 15–30% of runtime. That's an estimate, not a measurement; see the test below.
3. **Mitigations that actually work:** 2 vCPUs not 16, no GPU passthrough, virtio-balloon, **no compositor in the guest** (just Falcon + work apps, waypipe out), and start/stop on demand rather than at boot. That converts always-on drain into drain-while-working.
4. **The real comparison isn't "VM vs no VM" — it's "VM on shiori vs carrying setsuna."** If the alternative is doing work on setsuna, shiori's battery was never the baseline. You're consolidating two laptops into one and shiori's battery now carries work's share. That's the price of the whole idea, and it's the only honest way to score it.

**Hardware's fine:** KVM present (`vmx`, `/dev/kvm`), 16 threads, 30GB RAM. `qemu`/`waypipe`/`swtpm` are all absent — net-new.

**Two facts I couldn't establish from the repo, and one could kill the plan:**

- **Arch is not a CrowdStrike-supported distro,** and this repo contains *zero* Falcon config — only an Okta bookmark (`home.nix:1351`). So whatever Falcon you run on setsuna is installed out-of-band. If it's a repackaged `.deb`/`.rpm`, the guest should be Ubuntu/Debian — which means the guest **isn't** a setsuna mirror, and "mirrors setsuna" becomes "runs the work apps" instead.
- **Device trust may reject a VM.** If your posture check is TPM-bound, the guest needs a vTPM (`swtpm`), and some IT configs refuse virtualised hosts outright. Not worth building anything until this is known.

**Next action (~2 min): get the battery baseline so point 2 stops being a guess.**

```
cat /sys/class/power_supply/BAT0/power_now
```

That's µW at your current idle. Note it; we compare against it once a guest is running. Then tell me how Falcon is actually installed on setsuna (AUR? vendor `.deb`? does setsuna even run it?) — that decides guest distro, and it's the last thing blocking a concrete plan.

content.text:
Yes on both counts — and this is the design that actually works. You already own the box: **setsuna.**

**Why setsuna, not a new one**

1. It's already `gui = true` in `flake.nix:69`, already runs this flake, already work-connected, already has Falcon however you installed it. Zero new hosts, zero Falcon packaging work, zero flake changes on the Falcon side.
2. **Don't use fujiwara.** It's `gui = false`, and in this repo that swaps gnome-keyring for pass-secret-service (`home.nix:25-29`) — while Slack's Electron safeStorage wants libsecret (`home.nix:145-146`). Plus no graphical session has run on it since Jun 2025. setsuna avoids that whole wrinkle.

**Yes, Slack lands here as a real window**

`waypipe ssh setsuna slack`. Slack's process runs on setsuna; waypipe proxies the Wayland protocol back so it's an ordinary Hyprland window on shiori — not a nested desktop rectangle. It's packaged both ways: `extra/waypipe` 0.11.2, nixpkgs 0.11.0. No compositor needed on setsuna — waypipe's remote side *is* the Wayland socket the app connects to.

**The property that makes this correct, not just convenient:** the Slack process and its network connection originate from setsuna, so device trust sees a compliant host. Slack *web* on shiori would likely be **blocked** for exactly the reason you gave — no Falcon here. And Falcon never touches shiori's disk at all. Separate machine, separate kernel, separate disk: stronger than the VM on every axis, and the battery question disappears because nothing work-related runs locally.

**Three honest weak points**

3. **Audio does not traverse waypipe.** It's Wayland-only. Huddles and calls need PipeWire-over-network wired separately, or you take calls on setsuna directly. This is the real gap.
4. **Latency.** Fine on LAN. Over Tailscale WAN, Electron scrolling and typing degrade noticeably — Slack is a heavy client.
5. **Screen sharing captures setsuna, not shiori.** So anything you need to *show* has to live on setsuna too. That's the logical consequence of the boundary you asked for, and it's worth deciding now rather than discovering in a meeting.

**Next action (~2 min):** confirm setsuna is reachable and note whether the tailscale CLI is even on PATH — it wasn't found on shiori:

```
ssh setsuna true && echo reachable
```

Then say go and I'll add `pkgs.waypipe` to `home.nix` for both hosts in a worktree, and we'll smoke-test with something light (`foot`) before pointing it at Slack. Per repo policy that's commit + push + `hms`, so budget ~10 min of CI per host.

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/tdd

# TDD

## Overview

**Test-first, always.** Write the failing test before the code it covers, watch
it fail, then write the minimal code to make it pass. A test you never saw fail
proves nothing — it may pass for the wrong reason, or not exercise the behavior
at all.

Keep the test scoped to the interfaces you are actually changing — a test that
drifts wider stops being a contract anyone can rely on. Inside a drovr phase
this also binds the next phase's contract.

## The cycle

1. **RED** — write the failing test named in the task's verification. Run it.
   *Watch it fail*, and confirm it fails for the reason you expect (missing
   behavior, not a typo or compile error elsewhere).
2. **GREEN** — write the *minimal* code to make that test pass. No extra
   features, no speculative abstraction — just enough to go green.
3. **REFACTOR** — clean up with the test as your safety net, re-running it.

Repeat per behavior. One failing test at a time.

## Red flags — STOP

- Wrote code before the test → delete it, start with the test.
- "I'll add the test after" → tests-after check *what the code does*, not what it
  *should* do. Test first.
- Test passed the first time you ran it → you never saw RED; make sure it truly
  exercises the new behavior.
- Test is scoped wider than this task's interfaces → tighten it; drift breaks the
  contract the next phase inherits.

## Verifying the pass

Green on the one test is necessary, not sufficient. Before claiming done, hand
off to `drovr:verification-before-completion` — run the full suite and the build,
and confirm with evidence, not assertion.

**Verdict: latency won't be your problem. Your leg is healthy.**

1. **RTT to your AP: 2.03ms avg** (min 1.53 / max 5.0), **jitter 0.85ms, 0% loss** over 30 packets.

**What that number does *not* cover, in order of how likely it is to bite:**

4. **Airtime contention.** Both boxes on one AP share the same radio. A big Electron repaint burst competes with your own traffic, so the bad case is throughput-under-load, not idle RTT. 30 packets on an idle link is also a small sample — WiFi failures are bursty, so this is a green light, not a clean bill of health.
5. **Audio still doesn't traverse waypipe** (unchanged from before), and if utsuho associates to 2.4GHz or a different AP, every number above changes.

**Next action: power utsuho on and tell me.** Then I'll measure the real thing — RTT/jitter between the two boxes, plus an SSH throughput probe to size the repaint headroom — before I touch `home.nix`. **Found it.** utsuho is on `10.0.0.101/20` via `wlan0`, default via `10.0.0.1` — **the same subnet as shiori.** The DERP relay is the mechanism, and now I know why:

- **`MappingVariesByDestIP: true`** — symmetric NAT, which defeats UDP hole punching.
- fujiwara's ARP entry for `10.0.0.101` was **`FAILED`** (visible in its neighbour table earlier) — no L2 path from the wired side.

But shiori and utsuho are *both* wireless clients on the same AP. Testing the path that skips tailscale and fujiwara entirely:

content.text:
**Verdict: the transport is the blocker, not the design. Don't build yet.** Full measurement set:

| path | result |
|---|---|
| shiori → AP gateway | 2.03ms avg, 0.85ms jitter, 0% loss |
| shiori → fujiwara (wired) | **1.86ms** avg, 0.41ms jitter, 0% loss |
| shiori → utsuho (wireless, same /20) | **100% loss, "No route to host"** |
| fujiwara → utsuho (DERP sfo) | **52ms avg, min 17, max 334, jitter 68ms** |

**Two independent causes, and the diagnosis is clean:**

1. **AP client isolation.** shiori and utsuho are both in `10.0.0.0/20` and cannot exchange a single packet. But shiori→fujiwara is 1.86ms — so **wireless→wired is permitted and wireless→wireless is blocked.** That's textbook client isolation on your AP.
2. **Symmetric NAT** (`MappingVariesByDestIP: true`). Tailscale can't hole-punch, and with no LAN path either it has nothing left, so DERP-via-SFO isn't a fallback — it's the permanent state. `Addrs = None` was the symptom.

52ms average with 68ms jitter and 334ms spikes is not viable for an Electron app over waypipe. My earlier ~10–20ms estimate assumed a direct path; that assumption is dead, and with it the jump-through-fujiwara plan as currently wired.

**Next action (~2 min, and it likely fixes everything): plug utsuho into ethernet.** The evidence says wired clients are reachable — fujiwara proves it at 1.86ms. A wired utsuho should land in the same range, which puts you comfortably inside waypipe's budget. The alternative fix is disabling client isolation on the AP, which is a router setting and helps both boxes.

Tell me when it's plugged in and I'll re-measure end to end (RTT, jitter, and an SSH throughput probe to size Electron repaints) before touching `home.nix`.

**Status: design settled** — utsuho as the work box, waypipe for Slack windows on shiori, nested `ssh fujiwara → ssh utsuho` as the transport since waypipe needs only a stdio pipe and fujiwara has `AllowTcpForwarding no`. **Nothing written to the repo, no worktree, no commits.** The TDD red test for the launcher waits on a transport worth building against.

You're right — I misread the topology, and two of my conclusions were wrong.

**The correction:** your office LAN uses the same private range as your home LAN — `10.0.0.0/20`, gateway `10.0.0.1`. So when utsuho reported `10.0.0.101/20`, I read that as "same subnet as shiori" when it's **address-space overlap between two different networks**. The "No route to host" was just unanswered ARP for a host that isn't on this LAN. There is no client isolation, and "plug utsuho into ethernet" was useless advice about a machine in another building. Scratch both.

**What survives, and it's the number that matters:** utsuho is remote, so the only path is WAN, and it's **permanently DERP-relayed** — 52ms avg, 68ms jitter, 334ms spikes, because the office NAT is symmetric (`MappingVariesByDestIP: true`). That measurement was always the real WAN path; I just attached the wrong explanation to it.

**So the waypipe-to-utsuho plan is dead.** It assumed a LAN-local work box. Piping Electron over a 68ms-jitter relay is a bad remote-desktop experience, and the jitter is not fixable from your side — it's the office's NAT.

**Which makes "really I want a new machine" the correct answer, not just the preferred one.** A work box *at home* gives you:

1. **~2ms, 0.4ms jitter** — fujiwara already demonstrates that number on your own network.
2. Falcon on real hardware with a real kernel, so device trust is satisfied and work access works.
3. Zero battery cost on shiori, because nothing work-related runs locally.
4. Your personal home on shiori is untouchable — separate machine, separate kernel, separate disk. Stronger than the VM I was proposing earlier.
5. It needs almost nothing: it renders Electron and runs Falcon. A mini-PC on mains beats a laptop, and no GPU passthrough is involved.

The main constraint is that it probably has to be **company-issued** to enroll in device trust — so the real move is asking IT to replace setsuna, ideally with a small desktop rather than a laptop since it never leaves your desk. Worth also flagging: that `10.0.0.0/20` overlap will bite any future subnet-routing setup between home and office, so avoid plans that need it.

**One thing I'd note for whatever you get:** Arch isn't a CrowdStrike-supported distro, so let the new box run whatever your Falcon package targets (Ubuntu LTS, most likely) and join this repo via home-manager only — keep it out of `system/deploy`'s allow-list (`system/deploy:62`), which is pacman-based and whose own comment says a box we don't own the OS of must not be handed packages.

**Next action:** tell me which you want and I'll start — (a) the flake/home-manager side for a new work host, which is additive and cheap to write now even before hardware lands, or (b) a local Falcon VM on shiori if you want something working before IT moves.

Still nothing written to the repo — no worktree, no commits.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about CrowdStrike Falcon macOS sensor and its Endpoint Security Framework system extension requirements:

## Technology Transition

The macOS version of the Falcon sensor uses a kernel extension (kext) on Intel Macs prior to Big Sur, but because of the limitations of kexts on Apple silicon, it now uses an endpoint security System Extension instead.

## Apple Silicon Support

All supported sensor versions include Intel CPUs and Apple silicon native support. For Apple Silicon, all macOS Versions are supported with CrowdStrike Custom Settings.

## System Extension Requirements

Apple requires system extensions to be approved before they can be loaded. System extension requirements include the Falcon system extension and Falcon non-removable system extension (macOS Sequoia 15 and later), as well as Falcon network filter extension.

## Full Disk Access

The Falcon sensor for Mac requires Full Disk Access (FDA) to Falcon as an additional authorization on each host. If Full Disk Access is not enabled, the sensor enters reduced functionality mode (RFM).

## Deployment Considerations

The CrowdStrike Settings Profiles approve CrowdStrike for network content filters, kernel extensions, system extensions, PPPC, and web-filtering requirements. This profile is compatible with both the older Falcon agent using kernel extensions and the latest version using system extensions.

The Falcon sensor for Mac requires Full Disk Access (FDA) to Falcon as an additional authorization on each host. If Full Disk Access is not enabled, the sensor enters reduced functionality mode (RFM).

## Deployment Considerations

The CrowdStrike Settings Profiles approve CrowdStrike for network content filters, kernel extensions, system extensions, PPPC, and web-filtering requirements. This profile is compatible with both the older Falcon agent using kernel extensions and the latest version using system extensions.

**Network-wise mari is the best box you have. But waypipe can't touch it.**

**Verified good:**

1. **mari is at home with a direct path** — `CurAddr = 10.0.10.70:41641`, no DERP. **3.74ms avg, 0.24ms jitter, 0% loss** from fujiwara; `tailscale ping` says 3ms direct. That's ~14x better than utsuho's relayed path.
2. **Falcon supports macOS properly.** On Apple Silicon it ships as an Endpoint Security **System Extension** rather than a kext, with native arm64 support — so none of the Linux kernel-access problems apply. It's the cleanest Falcon story of any option in this conversation ([CrowdStrike macOS deployment](https://inventivehq.com/knowledge-base/crowdstrike/how-to-install-the-crowdstrike-falcon-sensor-on-macos), [eclecticlight on ESF](https://eclecticlight.co/2024/07/22/could-our-macs-be-crowdstruck/)).

**The fatal part: macOS has no Wayland, so waypipe is out.** waypipe proxies the Wayland protocol; Slack on macOS is a native Cocoa app, and there's no X11 path either. You cannot get an integrated Slack window on shiori's Hyprland from a Mac. What you *can* get is full-desktop remote — macOS Screen Sharing (built in, no extra software) at 3.7ms, which would be genuinely smooth. But it's a window containing mari's screen, not a Slack window in your compositor.

**And the cost is the thing you started this conversation trying to avoid:**

3. **Falcon on macOS requires Full Disk Access** or it drops to Reduced Functionality Mode. So corporate EDR with full disk read.
4. **Approving those system extensions requires an MDM profile** — corporate device management on the machine.
5. mari sits in *this* repo with your personal sops secrets and serves as your **aarch64 remote builder** (`flake.nix` pins it at `100.106.204.103`). Enrolling it points corporate MDM and a full-disk-access EDR at your personal Mac and your nix build path.

So it hinges on one fact I can't read off the repo: **is mari work-issued or your personal Mac?** Everything about how it appears here — personal sops, your own attic cache, your builder — says personal. If it's personal, mari reintroduces the exact problem you rejected distrobox for, just relocated. If it's actually work-issued, it's a strong option and the only thing you give up is integrated windows.

Tell me which, and I'll either plan it on mari or go back to the new-machine route.

*(Aside, cheap to fix: your tailnet has a stale duplicate — `mari` listed Online=False alongside the live `mari-1`.)*

Based on my web search results, here's what I found regarding Linux VNC clients and support for Apple Screen Sharing authentication:

## Apple Authentication Type 30

Type 30 sends DH parameters, derives an AES key from MD5 of the shared secret, and encrypts a 128-byte username/password block. content.text:
X forwarding can't do this, and the reason is structural rather than a config detail.

**X forwarding carries X11 protocol between an X client and an X server.** Slack for macOS is a native Cocoa app — it isn't an X11 client, so there's nothing for `ssh -X mari slack` to forward. macOS has no equivalent of waypipe or X forwarding at all: Quartz has no per-app remoting protocol, which is why Apple's own answer is display-based Screen Sharing. XQuartz only helps X11 apps, and Slack isn't one.

So **per-app windows requires the far end to be Linux.** That kills the mari plan as you want it — mari can only ever give you a whole-desktop window. I've stopped building the TigerVNC path; nothing was written.

**That reduces the whole conversation to one trade.** Your three requirements — per-app windows, healthy Falcon, low latency — can't all be met by any box you currently have:

| option | per-app windows | Falcon healthy | latency |
|---|---|---|---|
| mari (enrolled, ready now) | ✗ desktop only | ✓ | 10ms |
| utsuho (at the office) | ✓ Linux | ✓ | ✗ 52ms / 68ms jitter |
| **Linux VM on shiori** | ✓ | ✓ own kernel | ✓ **local, ~0ms** |
| new local Linux box | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ ~2ms |

**The VM is back, and this time it's the right answer** — I dismissed it too early on your battery objection. A VM has its own kernel, so Falcon loads its eBPF probes and reports healthy; it's Linux, so waypipe gives you real per-app Slack windows in Hyprland; and it's local, so there's no network leg at all. Your personal home stays unreachable — separate kernel, separate filesystem, and unlike distrobox there's no `$HOME` bind-mount to work around.

The cost is the one you flagged: ~2–5W, call it 15–30% of runtime, and only while it's running. Mitigations stand — 2 vCPUs, no compositor in the guest, no GPU passthrough, start/stop on demand.

One constraint carries over: **the guest should run a Falcon-supported distro (Ubuntu LTS most likely), not Arch.** So it joins this repo via home-manager only, and stays out of `system/deploy`'s pacman allow-list.

**Two ways forward — pick one and I'll start:**

1. **Build the VM** — microvm or plain qemu on shiori, Ubuntu guest, Falcon inside, waypipe out, `work` command to enter and to launch Slack. This is the only thing that meets all three requirements without buying hardware. Roughly a weekend, and the first milestone (guest boots, waypipe shows a window) is an evening.
2. **Ship mari now as a stopgap** — I was ~20 minutes from done: `pkgs.tigervnc` on shiori plus a `work` command. Whole-desktop, not per-app, but working today. You'd need to enable Screen Sharing on mari yourself (System Settings → General → Sharing); I'm not flipping a service-exposing setting on an enrolled machine for you.

Worth noting for (1): mari's address and the work-host identity belong in `dotfiles-private` (`endpoints.nix`), not hardcoded here — this repo is public, and that input exists for exactly these values.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for `work` (defined in home.nix), the launcher that runs work apps on the
# work host and brings their windows here over waypipe.
#
# The work host's address is deliberately NOT in this repo -- it is public, and an
# internal address is nobody else's business (see the dotfiles-private flake
# input). So the script resolves it at runtime from $WORK_HOST or a host file, and
# these cases drive that resolution through four override seams: WORK_HOST,
# WORK_HOST_FILE, WORK_SSH_BIN and WORK_WAYPIPE_BIN. Nothing here contacts a real
# host -- the ssh and waypipe stubs only record the argv they were handed.
#
#   ./tests/work.sh                 # builds the script, then tests it
#   ./tests/work.sh /path/to/script # tests one you already have
#
# Why a shell wrapper is worth testing at all: the whole point of the script is
# the *shape* of the command it execs (shell vs waypipe, argv order, where the
# host comes from), and that shape is exactly what silently regresses.
set -u

SCRIPT="${1:-}"
if [ -z "$SCRIPT" ]; then
  host=$(cat /etc/hostname)
  drv=$(nix eval --raw ".#homeConfigurations.$host.config.home.packages" \
    --apply 'ps: (builtins.head (builtins.filter (p: p.name or "" == "work") ps)).drvPath') \
    || { echo "could not evaluate work for $host" >&2; exit 1; }
  SCRIPT="$(nix-store --realise "$drv" | tail -1)/bin/work"
  echo "testing $SCRIPT"
fi
[ -x "$SCRIPT" ] || { echo "not executable: $SCRIPT" >&2; exit 1; }

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

# Stubs that record argv rather than exec anything. One file per stub so a case
# can assert which of the two was taken -- "ran ssh when it should have run
# waypipe" is the regression most worth catching.
for name in ssh waypipe; do
  cat > "$D/$name" <<STUB
#!/bin/sh
printf '%s\n' "\$*" > "$D/$name.argv"
exit 0
STUB
  chmod +x "$D/$name"
done

# Every invocation goes through run(), which clears the environment rather than
# inheriting it: WORK_HOST left exported while debugging would silently satisfy
# the cases that are supposed to fail for want of a host.
run() {
  rm -f "$D/ssh.argv" "$D/waypipe.argv"
  env -i PATH="$PATH" HOME="$D" \
    WORK_SSH_BIN="$D/ssh" WORK_WAYPIPE_BIN="$D/waypipe" \
    "$@" > "$D/stdout" 2> "$D/stderr"
  echo $? > "$D/rc"
}

ok() { n=$((n + 1)); printf 'ok   %s\n' "$1"; }
no() { n=$((n + 1)); fails=$((fails + 1)); printf 'FAIL %s\n     %s\n' "$1" "$2"; }

check() { # check <desc> <expected> <actual>
  if [ "$2" = "$3" ]; then ok "$1"; else no "$1" "expected [$2], got [$3]"; fi
}

argv() { cat "$D/$1.argv" 2>/dev/null || echo "<not called>"; }
rc() { cat "$D/rc"; }

# ── host resolution ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# No host anywhere: must refuse rather than guess, and must say how to fix it.
run "$SCRIPT" slack
check "no host configured exits 2" "2" "$(rc)"
if grep -qi "WORK_HOST" "$D/stderr"; then
  ok "no host configured names the env var"
else
  no "no host configured names the env var" "stderr: $(cat "$D/stderr")"
fi

# WORK_HOST is the simplest seam.
run WORK_HOST=workbox "$SCRIPT" slack
check "WORK_HOST reaches waypipe" "ssh workbox slack" "$(argv waypipe)"

# A host file is the persistent form, so the address lives outside this repo.
printf '# the work box\n\nworkbox-from-file\n' > "$D/hostfile"
run WORK_HOST_FILE="$D/hostfile" "$SCRIPT" slack
check "host file skips comments and blanks" "ssh workbox-from-file slack" "$(argv waypipe)"

# Precedence: an explicit env var beats the file.
run WORK_HOST=env-wins WORK_HOST_FILE="$D/hostfile" "$SCRIPT" slack
check "WORK_HOST beats the host file" "ssh env-wins slack" "$(argv waypipe)"

# ── which transport gets taken ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# No app: an interactive shell. waypipe proxies Wayland and has no business in a
# plain shell, so this must take ssh -t and leave waypipe untouched.
run WORK_HOST=workbox "$SCRIPT"
check "bare invocation runs ssh -t" "-t workbox" "$(argv ssh)"
check "bare invocation does not run waypipe" "<not called>" "$(argv waypipe)"

# An app: waypipe, and ssh must NOT be invoked directly -- waypipe runs it.
run WORK_HOST=workbox "$SCRIPT" slack
check "app invocation does not run ssh directly" "<not called>" "$(argv ssh)"

# Arguments after the app name belong to the app, in order.
run WORK_HOST=workbox "$SCRIPT" slack --startup --disable-gpu
check "app arguments pass through in order" \
  "ssh workbox slack --startup --disable-gpu" "$(argv waypipe)"

# ── usage ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

run WORK_HOST=workbox "$SCRIPT" --help
check "--help exits 0" "0" "$(rc)"
if grep -qi "usage" "$D/stdout"; then
  ok "--help prints usage to stdout"
else
  no "--help prints usage to stdout" "stdout: $(cat "$D/stdout")"
fi
check "--help runs nothing" "<not called>" "$(argv waypipe)"

printf '\n%d case(s), %d failure(s)\n' "$n" "$fails"
[ "$fails" -eq 0 ]

rc() { cat "$D/rc"; }

check "no host configured exits 2" "2" "$(rc)"
if grep -qi "WORK_HOST" "$D/stderr"; then
  ok "no host configured names the env var"
else

fi

check "WORK_HOST reaches waypipe" "ssh workbox slack" "$(argv waypipe)"

check "host file skips comments and blanks" "ssh workbox-from-file slack" "$(argv waypipe)"

check "bare invocation does not run waypipe" "<not called>" "$(argv waypipe)"

run WORK_HOST=workbox "$SCRIPT" slack
check "app invocation does not run ssh directly" "<not called>" "$(argv ssh)"

# Tell the lock screen when pam_faillock has the account locked out. hyprlock
  # forwards a PAM message only when it contains "left to unlock"
  # (src/auth/Pam.cpp), so PAM's own "The account is locked due to N failed
  # logins." is dropped, and the countdown that does survive shows up only after a
  # password has been submitted -- typing the right one and being rejected anyway
  # is how you find out. This reads the tally instead, so a label can say it up
  # front. No root needed: /run/faillock/$USER is mode 0660 owned by the user.
  hyprlock-faillock = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "hyprlock-faillock" ''
    set -u

    # The lock screen's lockout is enforced by the pam hyprlock links, not the host's:
    # nix libpam loads pam_faillock.so from its own lib/security, and that module has
    # its own faillock.conf path compiled in. So read THAT file -- reading
    # /etc/security/faillock.conf would report host policy while the lock screen went
    # on enforcing whatever nix's copy says (both are upstream's all-commented
    # default today, so the numbers agree, which is exactly why the divergence would
    # go unnoticed). Module arguments in /etc/pam.d/system-auth would override the
    # file for either pam and are invisible from here; the host's stack passes none.
    CONF="''${FAILLOCK_CONF:-${pkgs.pam-host-chkpwd}/etc/security/faillock.conf}"
    # Unreadable (a nixpkgs that stops installing it): read nothing, which lands on
    # pam built-in defaults -- the same thing read_config_file() leaves pam with.
    # Falling back to the host file would reintroduce exactly the divergence above.
    [ -r "$CONF" ] || CONF=/dev/null
=== packages list around 3040 ===
    # emacsclient, so gating this on the desktop stack breaks editing over SSH.
    #
    # withHostNss, not bare: an unwrapped nix emacs can't dlopen the host's
    # libnss_systemd.so.2, so getpwuid/getpwnam fail for a homed-only user with
    # no /etc/passwd entry. Emacs then sets init-file-user to "sauyon" instead
    # of "", can't resolve ~sauyon, and every startup warns "User sauyon has no
    # home directory" (startup.el's file-directory-p check). services.emacs
    # already wraps the daemon; the CLI on PATH needs it too.
    (withHostNss emacsPkg)
  ] ++ lib.optionals (!isDarwin && isDesktop) [
    caffeine
    # nixGL wrap: without it the FHS env resolves GBM/DRI via the NixOS-only
    # /run/opengl-driver path and falls back to software rendering.
    (config.lib.nixGL.wrap cumora)
    hypr-fullscreen-inhibit
    hypr-unstuck-lock
    # Also on PATH so a lockout can be checked (and waited out) from a TTY.
    hyprlock-faillock

    # Unaffected by the move off firefox: gecko asks for native manifests under
    # XREUserNativeManifests, which on Linux is a forced-legacy ~/.mozilla for
    # every gecko app no matter where its profile lives — so whatever

cat > /tmp/claude-1000/-home-sauyon-devel-dotfiles/420079fd-ff81-4808-a107-49091f80e00b/scratchpad/work-snippet.nix <<'NIXEOF'
  # Run a work app on the work host and show its window here, over waypipe.
  #
  # Why work stays on another machine: work access is gated on a healthy
  # CrowdStrike Falcon sensor, and Falcon needs privileges no container can give
  # it -- kprobe/tracepoint eBPF loads are checked against the INITIAL user
  # namespace, so a rootless container's capabilities do not count and the sensor
  # sits in Reduced Functionality Mode. distrobox is doubly wrong for it: it
  # bind-mounts $HOME unconditionally (distrobox-create's --volume "$HOME:$HOME"),
  # and --home only ADDS a second mount while exporting DISTROBOX_HOST_HOME at the
  # real one -- so the personal tree stays readable from inside either way.
  #
  # waypipe proxies the Wayland protocol rather than a framebuffer, so each app
  # arrives as an ordinary window in this compositor: X forwarding's ergonomics
  # without X. It carries no audio, so calls belong on the work host itself.
  #
  # The host's address is deliberately NOT in this repo -- it is public, and an
  # internal address is nobody else's business (see the dotfiles-private input).
  # $WORK_HOST wins, else the first non-comment line of $WORK_HOST_FILE.
  work = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "work" ''
    set -u

    SSH="''${WORK_SSH_BIN:-${pkgs.openssh}/bin/ssh}"
    WAYPIPE="''${WORK_WAYPIPE_BIN:-${pkgs.waypipe}/bin/waypipe}"
    HOST_FILE="''${WORK_HOST_FILE:-$HOME/.config/work/host}"

    usage() {
      ${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/printf '%s\n' \
        'usage: work [app [args...]]' \
        "" \
        '  work             interactive shell on the work host (ssh -t)' \
        '  work slack       run slack there; its window appears here via waypipe' \
        '  work <app> ...   arguments after <app> go to the app' \
        "" \
        'Host: $WORK_HOST, else the first non-comment line of $WORK_HOST_FILE' \
        '(default ~/.config/work/host).'
    }

    case "''${1:-}" in
      -h | --help) usage; exit 0 ;;
    esac

    HOST="''${WORK_HOST:-}"
    # Strip comments and whitespace, then take the first line with anything left.
    if [ -z "$HOST" ] && [ -r "$HOST_FILE" ]; then
      HOST=$(${pkgs.gnused}/bin/sed -e 's/#.*//' -e 's/[[:space:]]//g' "$HOST_FILE" \
        | ${pkgs.gnugrep}/bin/grep -m1 . || true)
    fi
    if [ -z "$HOST" ]; then
      echo "work: no work host set. Export WORK_HOST, or write it to $HOST_FILE" >&2
      exit 2
    fi

    # No app named: a plain shell, which waypipe has no part in.
    [ "$#" -eq 0 ] && exec "$SSH" -t "$HOST"

    # waypipe runs ssh itself and starts its own remote half, so the app's argv
    # follows the host. It needs waypipe on the FAR side's PATH too -- which the
    # isDesktop package block below provides, so a gui = false work host would
    # need waypipe added for it explicitly.
    exec "$WAYPIPE" ssh "$HOST" "$@"
  '';

NIXEOF
echo "snippet written: $(wc -l < /tmp/claude-1000/-home-sauyon-devel-dotfiles/420079fd-ff81-4808-a107-49091f80e00b/scratchpad/work-snippet.nix) lines"

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.

Clean, all four angles delivered, two **nit** findings — neither gates the Iron Law. But the first is a real cheap hardening, so I'll fix it (test first), and the second I'll decline with a recorded reason.

The `set -e` suggestion is actually a latent bug: under `set -e`, the `[ "$#" -eq 0 ] && exec ...` guard would exit the script whenever an app *is* named, breaking `work slack` entirely.

h = "home.nix"

a2 = '''    if [ -z "$HOST" ]; then
      echo "work: no work host set. Export WORK_HOST, or write it to $HOST_FILE" >&2
      exit 2
    fi
'''
assert s.count(a2) == 1
n2 = a2 + '''    # A leading hyphen would reach ssh as a flag rather than a hostname, and
    # -oProxyCommand=... is a command. The file is the user's own, so this is
    # self-injection only; it is still free to refuse.
    case "$HOST" in
      -*)
        echo "work: refusing a host that looks like an option: $HOST" >&2
        exit 2
        ;;
    esac
'''
s = s.replace(a2, n2, 1)
open(h, "w").write(s)
print("both patched")
PY

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# Cases for `work` (defined in home.nix), the launcher that runs work apps on the
3	# work host and brings their windows here over waypipe.
4	#
5	# The work host's address is deliberately NOT in this repo -- it is public, and an
6	# internal address is nobody else's business (see the dotfiles-private flake
7	# input). So the script resolves it at runtime from $WORK_HOST or a host file, and
8	# these cases drive that resolution through four override seams: WORK_HOST,
9	# WORK_HOST_FILE, WORK_SSH_BIN and WORK_WAYPIPE_BIN. Nothing here contacts a real
10	# host -- the ssh and waypipe stubs only record the argv they were handed.
11	#
12	#   ./tests/work.sh                 # builds the script, then tests it
13	#   ./tests/work.sh /path/to/script # tests one you already have
14	#
15	# Why a shell wrapper is worth testing at all: the whole point of the script is
16	# the *shape* of the command it execs (shell vs waypipe, argv order, where the
17	# host comes from), and that shape is exactly what silently regresses.
18	set -u
19	
20	SCRIPT="${1:-}"
21	if [ -z "$SCRIPT" ]; then
22	  host=$(cat /etc/hostname)
23	  drv=$(nix eval --raw ".#homeConfigurations.$host.config.home.packages" \
24	    --apply 'ps: (builtins.head (builtins.filter (p: p.name or "" == "work") ps)).drvPath') \
25	    || { echo "could not evaluate work for $host" >&2; exit 1; }
26	  SCRIPT="$(nix-store --realise "$drv" | tail -1)/bin/work"
27	  echo "testing $SCRIPT"
28	fi
29	[ -x "$SCRIPT" ] || { echo "not executable: $SCRIPT" >&2; exit 1; }
30	
31	D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
32	fails=0; n=0
33	
34	# Stubs that record argv rather than exec anything. One file per stub so a case
35	# can assert which of the two was taken -- "ran ssh when it should have run
36	# waypipe" is the regression most worth catching.
37	for name in ssh waypipe; do
38	  cat > "$D/$name" <<STUB
39	#!/bin/sh
40	printf '%s\n' "\$*" > "$D/$name.argv"
41	exit 0
42	STUB
43	  chmod +x "$D/$name"
44	done
45	
46	# Every invocation goes through run(), which clears the environment rather than
47	# inheriting it: WORK_HOST left exported while debugging would silently satisfy
48	# the cases that are supposed to fail for want of a host.
49	run() {
50	  rm -f "$D/ssh.argv" "$D/waypipe.argv"
51	  env -i PATH="$PATH" HOME="$D" \
52	    WORK_SSH_BIN="$D/ssh" WORK_WAYPIPE_BIN="$D/waypipe" \
53	    "$@" > "$D/stdout" 2> "$D/stderr"
54	  echo $? > "$D/rc"
55	}
56	
57	ok() { n=$((n + 1)); printf 'ok   %s\n' "$1"; }
58	no() { n=$((n + 1)); fails=$((fails + 1)); printf 'FAIL %s\n     %s\n' "$1" "$2"; }
59	
60	check() { # check <desc> <expected> <actual>
61	  if [ "$2" = "$3" ]; then ok "$1"; else no "$1" "expected [$2], got [$3]"; fi
62	}
63	
64	argv() { cat "$D/$1.argv" 2>/dev/null || echo "<not called>"; }
65	rc() { cat "$D/rc"; }

content.content:
## NO EMAILS

**Never write an email address into anything.** Not into files, commit messages,
docs, notes, handoffs or scratch files — mine, colleagues', or service accounts.
This repo is public, and an address is a durable identifier that spreads: it
leaks the work/personal boundary, it enumerates people, and once written it gets
copied onward.

Refer to an account by its **role** — "the personal Google account", "the work
account", "the project's GCS service agent" — or record the command that
recovers the identity at read time (`gcloud config get-value account`) rather
than pasting its output. Role-based wording is better documentation anyway: "must
be the personal account, not the work one" survives an address change; a pasted
address does not.

If an address seems genuinely load-bearing, ask first.

The exception is the git identity already configured in `home.nix`, which git
requires and which is on every commit regardless.

## Commit and Push Policy

This is a personal dotfiles repo on `master`. When asked to commit and push, do both without asking for confirmation. The global "ask before public communications" rule does not apply here.

## Applying config: use `hms`, not `home-manager switch`

`hms` (defined in `home.nix`, documented in `README.md`) pushes, waits for the
commit's CI run on `forge.ko.ag`, then switches — so the switch is a download of
the closure the in-cluster runner built, not a local compile. Expect it to block
for ten-odd minutes. `hms --local` builds here instead.

It refuses on a dirty tree and on a checkout behind `origin/master`. **Both
refusals are the feature.** CI can only build a pushed commit, so do not route
around them with a bare `home-manager switch` — commit and push, or pass
`--local` deliberately and say that you did.

If a run goes red, `hms` prints the job's `error:` lines; read those rather than
re-running blind. Background on why CI is worth waiting for — and the 600s attic
transfer ceiling that made it unreliable for its first 61 runs — is in
`docs/ci-nix-home.md`.
